## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 21: Inference for comparing paired means](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inference-paired-means.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn why paired observations are analyzed through their differences, how to test and estimate the mean paired difference by simulation, with a randomization test that shuffles within each pair and a bootstrap interval, and how to check both against the t-distribution, using new-textbook prices at the UCLA Bookstore and on Amazon.

## Randomization and bootstrap for paired differences

"Two sets of observations are *paired* if each observation in one set has a special correspondence or connection with exactly one observation in the other dataset." This section finds the textbooks that have both a UCLA Bookstore price and an Amazon price, tests whether the mean difference could be chance by shuffling within each book, and estimates that difference with the bootstrap.

### Exercise 11

Under the null hypothesis, it does not matter which store a price came from. Replace the code in that chunk so that it sets a random seed and then makes one shuffle of the data under that null hypothesis, randomly swapping, or not, the two prices within each book. Print the shuffled differences. Render.

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-11-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(21)
textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "permute")
```

###

Swapping a book's two prices flips the sign of its difference, so the first book's \$0.52 became -\$0.52 while the second book's \$0.71 stayed put. "The change in the paired setting, however, is that the assignment happens *within* an observational unit (here, a car)."

### Exercise 12

Replace the code in that chunk so that it sets a random seed, then creates `null_dist`: the means of 10,000 such shuffles, each swapping the two prices within each book at random. Print `null_dist`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-12
#| echo: false

```

###

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-12-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(21)
null_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

null_dist
```

###

Every shuffle keeps each book's two prices together and only decides which store gets which. "Remember, if the null hypothesis is true, it will not matter which brand is put on which tire because the overall tread wear will be the same across pairs."

### Exercise 13

Replace the line that prints `null_dist` with code that calculates the p-value: the proportion of the shuffled means at least as far from zero, in either direction, as the observed mean difference. Render.

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-13
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-13-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(21)
null_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

null_dist |>
  get_p_value(obs_stat = mean(textbooks$price_diff), direction = "two-sided")
```

###

Our p-value is 0.021; yours will differ slightly with a different seed. The alternative is two-sided, "$H_A:$ $\mu_{diff} \neq 0.$ There is a difference in average prices," so shuffled means below -\$3.58 count as evidence too.

### Exercise 14

Replace the p-value code with code that creates `boot_dist`: the means of 10,000 bootstrap resamples of the 68 price differences. Then calculate a 99% bootstrap percentile confidence interval from `boot_dist`. Keep the seed and `null_dist` above it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-14
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: randomization-and-bootstrap-for-paired-differences-14-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(21)
null_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_dist |>
  get_confidence_interval(level = 0.99, type = "percentile")
```

###

Our interval runs from \$0.05 to \$8.28; the chapter's, from 1,000 resamples, runs from \$0.25 to \$7.87. "That is, the original dataset would include the list of 68 price differences, and each resample will also include 68 price differences (some repeated through the bootstrap resampling process)."

## Mathematical model for the mean paired difference

"Thinking about the differences as a single observation on an observational unit changes the paired setting into the one-sample setting." This section checks the simulations against the t-distribution, and then shows what is lost when the pairing is ignored.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that calculates, for `price_diff`, the number of pairs, the mean, the standard deviation, and the standard error: the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of pairs. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-1-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean = mean(price_diff),
            sd = sd(price_diff),
            se = sd / sqrt(n))
```

###

The chapter's numbers exactly: 68 pairs, a mean of \$3.58, a standard deviation of \$13.42, and a standard error of \$1.63. "Note that instead of reporting the prices separately for UCLA and Amazon, the summary statistics are given by the mean of the differences, the standard deviation of the differences, and the total number of pairs (i.e., differences)."

### Exercise 2

Add a column with the bootstrap's estimate of the same standard error: the standard deviation of the means in `boot_dist`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-2-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean = mean(price_diff),
            sd = sd(price_diff),
            se = sd / sqrt(n),
            boot_se = sd(boot_dist$stat))
```

###

The formula and our 10,000 bootstrap resamples agree, both at \$1.63; the chapter's 1,000 resamples gave \$1.64. Simulation and formula measure the same thing: how much the mean difference would vary from sample to sample.

### Exercise 3

The t-model's first condition is "Independently sampled pairs." Replace the code in that chunk so that it shows the rows of `textbooks` whose `textbook_isbn` appears more than once. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-3-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = textbook_isbn) |>
  arrange(textbook_isbn)
```

###

Nine books appear twice, each used by two cross-listed courses or by two courses in a sequence, so 18 of the 68 pairs come from just 9 books. The chapter says "This is a simple random sample, so assuming the textbooks are independent seems reasonable," but the sample was of courses, not books, and one book even has two different Amazon prices.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates the T score: the mean difference minus the null value of 0, divided by the standard error. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-5-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  summarize(mean = mean(price_diff),
            se = sd(price_diff) / sqrt(n())) |>
  mutate(t = (mean - 0) / se)
```

###

The T score is 2.20, the chapter's value. "The T score is a ratio of how the sample mean difference varies from zero as compared to how the observations vary."

### Exercise 6

Add a column with the p-value: twice the area beyond that T score in one tail of a t-distribution with 67 degrees of freedom. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-6-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  summarize(mean = mean(price_diff),
            se = sd(price_diff) / sqrt(n())) |>
  mutate(t = (mean - 0) / se,
         p_value = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = 67))
```

###

"Doubling this area gives the p-value: 0.0312." The randomization test gave us 0.021; both are below 0.05, and "When the null hypothesis is true and the conditions are met, T has a t-distribution with $df = n_{diff} - 1.$"

### Exercise 7

Replace the code in that chunk with a one-sample t-test of `price_diff` against a null value of 0, done by a single function built for it. Render.

```{r}
textbooks |>
  t_test(response = price_diff, mu = 0)
```

The test gives the same T score, 2.20, the same 67 degrees of freedom, and the same p-value, 0.0312. "It is worth noting that if mathematical modeling is chosen as the analysis tool, paired data inference on the difference in measurements will be identical to the one-sample mathematical techniques," those of Chapter 19 on a single mean.

### Exercise 8

To see what the pairing buys, ignore it. Replace the code in that chunk so that it reshapes `textbooks` so that each price is its own row, labeled by store, and then runs a two-sample t-test comparing the bookstore prices with the Amazon prices as if they came from two independent groups. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-8-test
#| echo: true
textbooks |>
  pivot_longer(c(bookstore_new, amazon_new),
               names_to = "store", values_to = "price") |>
  t_test(price ~ store, order = c("bookstore_new", "amazon_new"))
```

###

The estimate is the same \$3.58, but the p-value jumps to 0.707, because the \$55 spread between books now swamps the \$13 spread within them; the help page's claim of "no statistical difference" matches this unpaired test, not the paired one. "That said, depending on how the data are collected, we don't always have mechanism for pairing the data and reducing the inherent variability across observations."

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk so that it finds $t^\star$ for a 95% and for a 99% confidence interval: the cutoffs on a t-distribution with 67 degrees of freedom that leave 2.5% and 0.5% in each tail. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-9-test
#| echo: true
tibble(level = c(0.95, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(t_star = qt(1 - (1 - level) / 2, df = 67))
```

###

The cutoffs are 2.00 and 2.65, a little wider than the normal model's 1.96 and 2.58. "The margin of error is $t^\star_{df} \times s_{diff}/\sqrt{n_{diff}}$ where $t^\star_{df}$ is calculated from a specified percentile on the t-distribution with *df* degrees of freedom."

### Exercise 10

Add columns for the lower and upper ends of each confidence interval: the chapter's point estimate, 3.58, plus and minus $t^\star$ times the chapter's standard error, 1.63. Render.

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: mathematical-model-for-the-mean-paired-difference-10-test
#| echo: true
tibble(level = c(0.95, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(t_star = qt(1 - (1 - level) / 2, df = 67),
         lower = 3.58 - t_star * 1.63,
         upper = 3.58 + t_star * 1.63)
```

###

"We are 95% confident that the UCLA Bookstore is, on average, between \$0.32 and \$6.84 more expensive than Amazon for UCLA course books." The 99% interval, -\$0.74 to \$7.90, includes zero, which agrees with a p-value of 0.031: below 0.05 but above 0.01.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 21: Inference for comparing paired means](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inference-paired-means.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned why paired observations are analyzed through their differences, how to test and estimate the mean paired difference by simulation, with a randomization test that shuffles within each pair and a bootstrap interval, and how to check both against the t-distribution, using new-textbook prices at the UCLA Bookstore and on Amazon.

The chapter's own summary, in the authors' words:

> Like the two independent sample procedures in [Chapter 20], the paired difference analysis can be done using a t-distribution. The randomization test applied to the paired differences is slightly different, however. Note that when randomizing under the paired setting, each null statistic is created by randomly assigning the group to a numerical outcome **within** the individual observational unit. The procedure for creating a confidence interval for the paired difference is almost identical to the confidence intervals created in [Chapter 19] for a single mean.

For the one-sample methods that paired data reduce to, read [Chapter 19: Inference for a single mean](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inference-one-mean.html), which the chapter points to in its first paragraph. For more on paired tests in R, see the **infer** article "[Tidy inference for paired data](https://infer.tidymodels.org/articles/paired.html)," which explains the within-pair shuffle you used.

````{verbatim}
---
title: "Inference for Comparing Paired Means"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(infer)
```

```{r}
textbooks <- ucla_textbooks_f18 |>
  select(subject, course_num, textbook_isbn, bookstore_new, amazon_new) |>
  filter(!is.na(bookstore_new), !is.na(amazon_new)) |>
  mutate(price_diff = bookstore_new - amazon_new)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
set.seed(21)
null_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  hypothesize(null = "paired independence") |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_dist <- textbooks |>
  specify(response = price_diff) |>
  generate(reps = 10000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")
```

```{r}
null_dist |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "gray75", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * mean(textbooks$price_diff),
             color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Shuffling Prices Within Each Textbook",
       subtitle = "Only 2% of shuffles give a mean difference as far from $0 as the observed $3.58",
       x = "Mean Price Difference, UCLA Bookstore - Amazon",
       y = "Count",
       caption = "10,000 within-book shuffles of 68 textbooks; UCLA courses, Fall 2018 (openintro)")
```

```{r}
boot_dist |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.25,
                 fill = "gray75", color = "white") +
  geom_function(fun = \(x) dt((x - 3.58) / 1.63, df = 67) / 1.63,
                color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.33, 6.83), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "UCLA Bookstore Versus Amazon, New Textbooks",
       subtitle = "Bootstrap and t-model agree: the bookstore charged $0.33 to $6.83 more on average",
       x = "Mean Price Difference, UCLA Bookstore - Amazon",
       y = "Density",
       caption = "10,000 bootstrap resamples of 68 textbooks; UCLA courses, Fall 2018 (openintro)")
```
````

###

"As with a two-sample analysis, quantitative measurements are made on each of two different levels of the explanatory variable." Your page shows both halves of the paired design: two prices for every book, analyzed as one difference.
